stem: (a) In a closed economy income tax is tY, government must balance its budget G=tY, consumption is proportional to disposable income and investment is exogenous. (i) Why is G endogenous? (ii) Compare its multiplier with fixed-G policy. (iii) How does higher t affect income? (b) C=100+1.3Y, I=500/r, money demand=150Y+100−1500r and money supply=2100. Is there an economically admissible IS–LM equilibrium?
answer: (a) G depends on Y; investment multiplier 1/[(1−c)(1−t)], larger than 1/[1−c(1−t)] for fixed G when t>0; higher t raises Y. (b) No equilibrium with Y≥0,r>0.
solution: Let C=c(1−t)Y, 0<c<1,0≤t<1. Goods balance gives Y=c(1−t)Y+I+tY, hence Y=I/[(1−c)(1−t)]. G is endogenous because income determines tax revenue and spending. With G held exogenous, the autonomous-spending multiplier is 1/[1−c(1−t)]. Its denominator exceeds the balanced-budget denominator by t, so the latter multiplier is larger. Raising t shifts spending from households, who spend only fraction c, to government, who spends all receipts; dY/dt>0 for I>0. In (b), IS requires −.3Y=100+500/r, impossible for nonnegative Y and positive r. LM is r=Y/10−4/3. Even allowing negative r does not produce a nonnegative-Y intersection: substitution into IS yields .03Y²+9.6Y+1100/3=0, whose terms are all nonnegative for Y≥0.
hint: Substitute the budget rule into goods balance before comparing multipliers.

stem: Two firms have cost C(q)=mq, inverse demands p₁=a−q₁−sq₂ and p₂=a−q₂−sq₁, where 0<s<1 and a>m>0. (a) Find Cournot quantities. (b) Derive direct demand functions. (c) Find Bertrand prices.
answer: Cournot q₁=q₂=(a−m)/(2+s). Interior direct demands qᵢ=[a(1−s)−pᵢ+spⱼ]/(1−s²). Bertrand p₁=p₂=[a(1−s)+m]/(2−s).
solution: Cournot profit is (a−m−qᵢ−sqⱼ)qᵢ. Its first-order condition is 2qᵢ+sqⱼ=a−m, giving the symmetric quantities. Inverting the 2×2 inverse-demand system gives q₁=[a(1−s)−p₁+sp₂]/(1−s²) and its counterpart. These formulas apply when both demands are positive; outside that region nonnegativity requires appropriate corner demand. In Bertrand competition maximize (pᵢ−m)qᵢ. The interior first-order condition is a(1−s)−2pᵢ+spⱼ+m=0. Solving the two conditions gives p=[a(1−s)+m]/(2−s)>m and positive demand. Own-price profit curvature is −2/(1−s²)<0.
hint: Invert the inverse-demand matrix before solving the price game.

stem: (a) A monopolist has TC=5+3(Q_A+Q_B), inverse demands P_A=15−Q_A and P_B=25−2Q_B, and can discriminate across separated markets. Find prices, quantities, profit and deadweight loss. (b) An airline optimally sells 1500 business tickets at Rs 200 and 6000 economy tickets at Rs 80. Both demand curves are linear and MC=Rs 50. Derive both demands and find uniform-price equilibrium if discrimination is disallowed.
solution: (a) Set market marginal revenues equal to MC=3: 15−2Q_A=3 and 25−4Q_B=3. Profit is (9−3)6+(14−3)5.5−5=91.5. Efficient quantities at price 3 are 12 and 11. The lost-surplus triangles are (1/2)(12−6)(9−3)=18 and (1/2)(11−5.5)(14−3)=30.25, totaling 48.25. (b) If P=A−bQ, then MR=P−bQ=50 at the observed optimum. Business b=(200−50)/1500=.1,A=350; economy b=(80−50)/6000=.005,A=110. For a uniform price p≤110, total demand is Q=25500−210p. Maximizing (p−50)Q gives p=(25500+210·50)/420=600/7 and the stated market quantities. This earns profit 1875000/7≈267857, more than the best business-only regime (p=200,Q=1500,profit225000), so it is globally optimal.
hint: Use MR=MC separately, then check both segments of the aggregate uniform-price demand.

stem: A competitive economy has X₁=√(L₁K), X₂=√(L₂T), fixed positive K,T and total labour L₁+L₂=L, with labour mobile between sectors. Relative demand is D₁/D₂=γ(p₁/p₂)^−2. (a) Relate X₁/X₂ to p₁/p₂. (b) How does equilibrium relative price change when γ increases?
answer: Relative supply X₁/X₂=(K/T)(p₁/p₂); equilibrium p₁/p₂=(γT/K)^(1/3), which rises with γ.
solution: Equal wages imply p₁√K/(2√L₁)=p₂√T/(2√L₂). Thus L₁/L₂=(p₁/p₂)²K/T. Substituting into the output ratio gives X₁/X₂=√[(L₁/L₂)(K/T)]=(p₁/p₂)K/T. Market clearing equates this to γ(p₁/p₂)^−2, so the relative price cubed is γT/K. Higher relative demand raises the relative price with elasticity 1/3.
hint: Equate value marginal products of mobile labour.

stem: An open IS–LM economy has flexible exchange rate e (domestic currency per foreign unit), no capital mobility, fixed domestic and foreign price levels P,P*, and balanced trade in equilibrium. The source prints TB=T̄+βP*/P−mY, T̄,β,m>0, while saying e adjusts to balance trade. (a) Derive the Y–r relation and compare it with closed-economy IS; describe LM. (b) What do higher G do to Y and e? (c) What does higher P* do to Y and e?
answer: The printed TB equation omits e and cannot determine its adjustment. If the intended term is βeP*/P, balanced trade gives the ordinary closed-economy IS; higher G raises Y,r and depreciates e, while higher P* leaves Y,r unchanged and lowers e proportionally.
solution: Literally the printed TB=0 fixes Y=(T̄+βP*/P)/m independently of e. Since e appears nowhere, its comparative statics cannot be obtained, and arbitrary IS/LM shifts may be incompatible with that fixed Y. Conditional on inserting the usual omitted e, TB=0 gives e=P(mY−T̄)/(βP*), requiring mY>T̄ for a positive rate. Goods balance then becomes Y=C(Y−T)+I(r)+G, identical to closed-economy IS because net exports are zero. With ordinary increasing money demand in Y and decreasing demand in r, fixed real balances give an upward-sloping LM. A rise in G shifts this IS right: its intersection with LM has higher Y and r. The trade-balance formula then requires higher e, a depreciation, to offset increased imports. Higher P* leaves IS and LM unchanged and hence leaves Y,r unchanged; e falls in inverse proportion to P*, keeping eP*/P constant.
hint: First check whether the exchange rate actually appears in the printed trade equation.
notes: Visual inspection of PDF page 13 confirms that e is missing from the printed TB equation. Conditional intended equation is clearly distinguished.

stem: (a) Technologies Y=min(K/3,L/2) and Y=min(K/2,L/3) each have marginal cost Rs 20 at the same competitive factor prices. Find the expansion path for Y=K^(2/3)L^(1/3). (b) A consumer buys X at its market price. Compare market purchase of Y with an alternative providing a fixed free ration of Y through government shops. Is the ration necessarily better for (i) strictly convex indifference curves, (ii) perfect substitutes, (iii) perfect complements?
answer: (a) Factor prices both 4; expansion path K=2L. (b) Under a ration-only alternative with no supplementary Y purchases, none of the three preference types guarantees improvement; the ration quantity matters.
solution: (a) With capital rental r and wage w, 3r+2w=20 and 2r+3w=20 give r=w=4. For Cobb–Douglas cost minimization MP_K/MP_L=2L/K=r/w=1, hence K=2L. (b) Let the ration be Ȳ, income M and X price pₓ; the free-ration allocation can have X=M/pₓ,Y=Ȳ. This may fail to match the original preferred bundle. For strictly convex preferences U=XY, M=pₓ=pᵧ=1, market optimum has utility 1/4, while free ration Ȳ=.1 yields utility .1. For substitutes U=X+Y, M=1,pₓ=2,pᵧ=1, market utility is 1 but the same ration gives .5+.1=.6. For complements U=min(X,Y), M=pₓ=pᵧ=1, market utility .5 exceeds ration utility .1. Large enough rations can improve each case. If supplementary Y purchases are permitted, the old affordable set is preserved (or expanded) and the consumer is weakly better off under all three types.
hint: Infer factor prices from both unit-cost equations; compare affordable sets under rationing.
notes: The answer distinguishes ration-only supply from a free allocation with optional supplementary market purchases, which the source does not specify.

stem: Explain whether each statement is true or false: (a) If higher own price increases demand, higher income reduces demand; by the same argument, if higher own price reduces demand, higher income increases demand. (b) A farmer earns all income by selling his crop at an exogenous price and consumes more crop when that price rises; therefore the crop is normal. (c) If higher non-wage income reduces labour supplied, higher wages must increase labour supplied. (d) ISI student stipends are part of GDP.
answer: (a) First implication true under standard assumptions, converse false. (b) True under the usual fixed-harvest model. (c) False. (d) False for stipends treated as transfers.
solution: (a) Slutsky gives x_p=h_p−x x_M, with h_p≤0. A positive x_p requires x_M<0, but negative x_p is possible for either normal or inferior goods, so the converse is invalid. (b) With a fixed harvest E and other-good price fixed, wealth is pE. Endowment Slutsky gives total dx/dp=h_p+(E−x)x_M. The farmer finances consumption from the harvest and has E−x≥0; therefore a positive total response requires x_M>0. If harvest itself responds to price, additional production assumptions are needed. (c) Normal leisure creates a negative income effect on labour; a wage rise also has a substitution effect toward work, so their net sign is ambiguous and labour supply may bend backward. (d) A stipend paid without a current productive service is a transfer, not payment for newly produced output. Educational services may enter GDP separately, but the transfer amount itself does not.
hint: Apply Slutsky with fixed income versus endowment income; distinguish transfers from production.
notes: (b) assumes a fixed crop endowment. (d) is the standard national-accounting classification of a stipend as a transfer, rather than remuneration for services.

stem: In the Solow model Y=√(KL), saving rate is .2 and labour growth .05. (a) Find steady capital/labour ratio, output and saving growth and wage. (b) If saving rises to .4, find the new steady output growth. (c) Compare output growth during transition with growth in the new steady state.
answer: With zero depreciation: old k*=16, wage 2, output and saving growth 5%; new k*=64, wage 4 and long-run output growth still 5%. Transition growth is above 5% and converges to it.
solution: No depreciation is supplied, so take δ=0. Per-worker dynamics are k̇=s√k−.05k. The old positive steady state satisfies √k=.2/.05=4, giving k=16 and competitive wage ∂Y/∂L=.5√k=2. With constant k, K,Y and S=sY all grow with L at 5%. Raising s to .4 gives k*=64 but does not alter long-run aggregate growth 5%. During adjustment from k=16, k rises, so g_Y=.05+(1/2)g_k>.05 until the limit. Immediately after the change g_K=s/√k=.10, hence g_Y=(g_K+g_L)/2=.075. As k approaches 64, g_Y approaches .05 from above; in continuous time the new steady state is approached asymptotically. If depreciation δ were specified, k*=[s/(.05+δ)]² and wages adjust accordingly.
hint: The saving rate changes the level of steady output per worker, not its long-run growth rate.
notes: Depreciation is not stated; zero depreciation is used explicitly.

stem: (a) A consumer has U=√[(x₁−s₁)(x₂−s₂)], s₁,s₂>0 and xᵢ≥sᵢ. Derive demands and budget shares under standard budget p₁x₁+p₂x₂≤M; are they linear in prices? (b) A symmetric utility function U(x₁,x₂)=U(x₂,x₁) is maximized subject to p(x₁+x₂)≤M. If the maximizer exists and is unique, prove x₁*=x₂*.
answer: (a) xᵢ=sᵢ+[M−p₁s₁−p₂s₂]/(2pᵢ); budget shares are 1/2+(pᵢsᵢ−pⱼsⱼ)/(2M), affine in prices at fixed M. Demands are generally nonlinear in prices. (b) Uniqueness plus symmetry forces equal quantities.
solution: (a) Feasibility requires M≥p₁s₁+p₂s₂. For strictly positive discretionary income E=M−p₁s₁−p₂s₂, write zᵢ=xᵢ−sᵢ; maximize √(z₁z₂) with discretionary budget E, giving pᵢzᵢ=E/2. Thus x₁=M/(2p₁)+s₁/2−p₂s₂/(2p₁), with the analogous expression for x₂. These are not jointly linear in prices because of reciprocals and price ratios. But p₁x₁/M=1/2+(p₁s₁−p₂s₂)/(2M) and the other share is analogous, so shares are affine in prices holding M fixed. At E=0 the only feasible bundle is subsistence. (b) If (a,b) is optimal, (b,a) is feasible and gives equal utility by symmetry. If a≠b this supplies two distinct maximizers, contradicting uniqueness. Hence a=b without requiring differentiability or concavity.
hint: Subtract subsistence expenditure; use swapping and uniqueness.

stem: (a) Two people have U_A=x_A1^α+x_A2^α, 0<α<1, and U_B=x_B1+x_B2. Derive the contract curve and its properties. (b) A firm has MC=AC=4 and demand q=100−10p. (i) Maximize revenue subject to profit at least 80. (ii) What if the target is 100? (iii) What if marginal cost rises to 8?
answer: (a) Interior contract curve x_A1=x_A2, completed by boundary segments when one aggregate stock binds. (b)(i) q=40,p=6. (ii) Target100 infeasible (maximum profit90). (iii) At MC8, maximum profit10, so targets80 and100 are infeasible.
solution: (a) Let total stocks be Ω₁,Ω₂>0. For any fixed total S=x_A1+x_A2, B utility is Ω₁+Ω₂−S. Strict concavity of t^α makes A prefer the most equal feasible division of S. Therefore efficient interior allocations have x_A1=x_A2. If Ω₁≤Ω₂, the complete curve is (t,t),0≤t≤Ω₁, plus (Ω₁,t),Ω₁≤t≤Ω₂; if Ω₂≤Ω₁, interchange labels. Any unequal nonboundary allocation permits a balancing transfer raising A utility without changing B utility. No point on the stated curve permits a Pareto improvement because raising A utility requires raising A total consumption and reducing B utility. (b) Inverse demand is p=10−q/10; revenue R=10q−q²/10, maximized without the constraint at q=50. Profit at MC4 is π=6q−q²/10. The target π≥80 restricts q to [20,40], where revenue is increasing; choose q=40,p=6. Maximum profit is 90 at q=30, so a target of 100 has no feasible output. At MC8, π=2q−q²/10 has maximum10 at q=10,p=9; thus even the old 80 target is impossible. If the profit constraint is dropped entirely, revenue maximization stays q=50,p=5 independently of cost, but would then lose money at MC8.
hint: For the contract curve, hold A’s total quantity fixed; for the firm, check profit feasibility before optimizing revenue.
